sections.section_title: Introduction to Why $h(t-\tau)$ Appears
sections.learning_goal: Explain that $h(t-\tau)$ appears because an impulse contribution located at time $\tau$ produces a time-shifted copy of the impulse response.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the section operates entirely on symbolic impulse-response notation.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Show how time invariance converts the response to $\delta(t)$ from $h(t)$ into the response to $\delta(t-\tau)$ as $h(t-\tau)$, then show how the input weight $x(\tau)d\tau$ scales that shifted response.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with a single impulse at a fixed location $\tau_0$, so the learner sees $\delta(t-\tau_0) \mapsto h(t-\tau_0)$ before generalizing to $\tau$.
paragraph_plan: State that convolution is built by tracking the output caused by one tiny input contribution at a time.
Recall the impulse-response fact $\delta(t) \mapsto h(t)$ for an LTI system.
Apply time invariance to move the impulse from $0$ to $\tau_0$, giving $\delta(t-\tau_0) \mapsto h(t-\tau_0)$.
Replace the fixed location $\tau_0$ with the running input location $\tau$.
Add the input weight $x(\tau)d\tau$ and identify $x(\tau)h(t-\tau)d\tau$ as one output contribution that will later be accumulated over all $\tau$.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the tutorial focused on why the shifted response is $h(t-\tau)$, not on evaluating a convolution integral or introducing the flip-shift procedure.

sections.section_title: Tracing the Response to an Impulse at $\tau$
sections.learning_goal: Map an impulse located at a specific time to the corresponding shifted impulse response of an LTI system.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the task is recognition of the symbolic time-shift pattern.

question_policy.answer_format: one shifted impulse-response expression

Confuse the input with the output, such as $\delta(t-4)$.

sections.section_title: Scaling the Shifted Response by $x(\tau)d\tau$

sections.section_title: Reading $h(t-\tau)$ at a Fixed Output Time

sections.section_title: Connecting Weighted Shifted Responses to the Convolution Integrand

State that positive products add area, negative products subtract area, and no overlap gives zero area.

sections.section_title: Interpreting the Product Area for a Fixed Output Time
sections.learning_goal: Given plots of $x(\tau)$ and $h(t_0-\tau)$ for one fixed output time, read the overlap interval, form the product height, and interpret the product area as $y(t_0)$.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Two aligned rectangular signal plots on the same $\tau$-axis for a fixed output time t0, with the overlap interval shaded and a small product-area panel below.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use visually simple intervals and integer heights so the example writer can focus on interpreting the overlap area, not algebraic setup.

question_policy.answer_format: signed numeric value for the fixed output, such as $y(2)=4$
question_policy.practice_question_model: A graph shows $x(\tau)=2$ on $0\le \tau\le 2$ and zero elsewhere, and $h(1-\tau)=1$ on $-1\le \tau\le 1$ and zero elsewhere. Interpret $y(1)$ as overlap area.
distractor_plan: Anticipate using the union length instead of the overlap length.
Anticipate forgetting to multiply the signal heights.
Anticipate reporting only the overlap interval rather than the area.
Anticipate treating t as a variable instead of the fixed output time.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: At fixed output time $t=2$, a graph shows $x(\tau)=1$ on $0\le \tau\le 3$ and $h(2-\tau)=2$ on $1\le \tau\le 4$, with both signals zero elsewhere. Interpret $y(2)$ as an overlap area.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Conclude that the overlap is $1\le \tau\le 3$, the product height is 2, and $y(2)=4$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the first active use of the tutorial schema for one fixed output time.
solution_step_plan: State that t is fixed at 2, so the only variable being scanned is $\tau$.
Read the support of $x(\tau)$ from the plot.
Read the support of $h(2-\tau)$ from the plot.
Find the overlap interval of the two supports.
Multiply the heights on the overlap and compute the rectangle area.
State the area as the convolution output value $y(2)$.
practice_variation_axes: Vary the fixed output time label.
Vary rectangular support endpoints while keeping one overlap interval.
Vary simple positive heights.
Keep the product as one rectangle.

sections.handoff_notes: The example should establish the fixed-t area-reading routine before adding sign or comparison wrinkles.

sections.section_title: Reading Positive Overlap Area from Two Positive Signals
sections.learning_goal: Recognize that when both overlapping signal values are positive, the product area contributes a positive amount to the convolution output.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Aligned plots of two positive finite-duration signals on a $\tau$-axis, with the overlap shaded and the positive product region shown above the axis.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use nonnegative rectangular signals with visible positive heights; keep all product values above the axis.

question_policy.answer_format: positive numeric output value
question_policy.practice_question_model: A graph shows $x(\tau)=1$ on $0\le \tau\le 5$ and $h(4-\tau)=3$ on $2\le \tau\le 4$, with both signals zero elsewhere. Use the positive overlap area to find $y(4)$.
distractor_plan: Anticipate giving a negative value despite both signals being positive.
Anticipate using only one signal height as the area.
Anticipate using the full width of one signal instead of the overlap width.
Anticipate adding heights instead of multiplying them.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: At fixed output time $t=3$, a graph shows $x(\tau)=2$ on $0\le \tau\le 4$ and $h(3-\tau)=1$ on $1\le \tau\le 3$, with both signals zero elsewhere. Use the overlap area to find $y(3)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the product is positive on the overlap and conclude that $y(3)=4$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Keeps the same fixed-time area routine but makes the sign of the output an explicit part of the interpretation.
solution_step_plan: Identify that both signal values are positive on the overlap.
Read the overlap interval from the plot.
Multiply the positive heights to get the positive product height.
Compute the positive rectangle area.
State that the positive area adds to the output value.
practice_variation_axes: Vary the positive heights.
Vary the overlap width.
Keep both signals entirely above the axis.
Use one clean rectangular product region.

sections.handoff_notes: Make the sign reasoning explicit; this prepares the next section where the product falls below the axis.

sections.section_title: Accounting for Signed Area When the Product Is Negative
sections.learning_goal: Recognize that when the overlapping signal values have opposite signs, the product area is below the axis and contributes a negative amount to the convolution output.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Aligned plots where $x(\tau)$ is positive on the overlap and $h(t-\tau)$ is negative on the same interval, with the product rectangle shaded below the axis.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use one positive rectangle and one negative rectangle so the sign of the product is visually unambiguous.

question_policy.answer_format: negative numeric output value
question_policy.practice_question_model: A graph shows $x(\tau)=3$ on $0\le \tau\le 2$ and $h(1-\tau)=-1$ on $1\le \tau\le 4$, with both signals zero elsewhere. Use the signed overlap area to find $y(1)$.
distractor_plan: Anticipate reporting the absolute area instead of the signed area.
Anticipate deciding the sign from only one signal rather than from the product.
Anticipate using the union of supports instead of the overlap.
Anticipate adding the amplitudes instead of multiplying them.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: At fixed output time $t=1$, a graph shows $x(\tau)=2$ on $0\le \tau\le 3$ and $h(1-\tau)=-1$ on $1\le \tau\le 4$, with both signals zero elsewhere. Use the signed overlap area to find $y(1)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the product is negative on $1\le \tau\le 3$ and conclude that $y(1)=-4$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Changes only the sign of one overlapping signal, so the same area routine now produces a negative output contribution.
solution_step_plan: Read the overlap interval from the two plotted supports.
Determine the sign of the product from the signs of the two signal values.
Compute the product height on the overlap.
Compute the rectangle area with its negative sign.
State the signed area as the output value.
practice_variation_axes: Vary which signal is negative on the overlap.
Vary the overlap width.
Vary simple positive and negative heights.
Keep the product region entirely below the axis.

sections.handoff_notes: Do not let the example become an integration-sign convention lesson; keep attention on signed area of the product.

sections.section_title: Comparing Output Values from Different Amounts of Overlap
sections.learning_goal: Compare two fixed-time convolution output values by comparing the signed product areas created by different amounts of overlap.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Two side-by-side fixed-time panels for the same $x(\tau)$ and shifted $h(t-\tau)$: one panel has a smaller overlap area and the other has a larger overlap area, with product regions shaded.
visual_elements: panel for first fixed output time
panel for second fixed output time
shaded product area in each panel
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use same-sign positive products in the first worked example so comparison depends on overlap amount before mixing in signed comparisons during later practice.

question_policy.answer_format: one comparison statement between fixed-time outputs
question_policy.practice_question_model: Two panels show the same $x(\tau)$ with $h(1-\tau)$ and $h(3-\tau)$. The product area for $t=1$ is a rectangle of area 2, and the product area for $t=3$ is a rectangle of area 6. Which comparison between $y(1)$ and $y(3)$ is correct?
distractor_plan: Include the reversed comparison.
Include equality based on the same signal heights.
Include a comparison based only on overlap width while ignoring product height.
Include a comparison that ignores signed area if a practice item includes a negative product.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Two panels show the same $x(\tau)$ with $h(1-\tau)$ and $h(3-\tau)$. Compare $y(1)$ and $y(3)$ by comparing the two overlap areas.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Conclude which output value is larger by comparing the signed product areas, not by comparing the shifted signals alone.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Uses the same overlap-area interpretation twice and asks for a comparison rather than one isolated output value.
solution_step_plan: Identify the fixed output time represented in each panel.
Read the overlap interval and product height for the first panel.
Read the overlap interval and product height for the second panel.
Compute or compare the signed product areas.
State the correct comparison between the two output values.
practice_variation_axes: Vary the two fixed output times.
Vary which panel has larger overlap.
Keep product signs positive first, then allow one signed-area comparison when visually clear.
Use rectangle areas so comparison does not require long computation.

sections.handoff_notes: The answer choices should be text comparisons, not diagram choices; the diagrams are problem data.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Zero Output from No Overlap Area
sections.learning_goal: Recognize that if $x(\tau)$ and $h(t_0-\tau)$ have no overlapping nonzero $\tau$-interval, then the product area is zero and $y(t_0)=0$.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Aligned $\tau$-axis plots where the support of $x(\tau)$ and the support of $h(t_0-\tau)$ are separated, with an explicit 'no overlap' gap and an empty product-area panel.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use separated rectangular supports so the absence of overlap is immediately visible; do not imply that the individual signal areas should be added.

question_policy.answer_format: zero output value
question_policy.practice_question_model: A graph shows $x(\tau)$ supported on $0\le \tau\le 2$ and $h(5-\tau)$ supported on $3\le \tau\le 4$, with no overlap. What is $y(5)$?
distractor_plan: Anticipate computing the area of one signal instead of the product area.
Anticipate using the gap length as an output value.
Anticipate multiplying heights despite no shared interval.
Anticipate assuming every fixed output time must produce a nonzero value.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: At fixed output time $t=5$, a graph shows $x(\tau)$ supported on $0\le \tau\le 2$ and $h(5-\tau)$ supported on $3\le \tau\le 4$. Use overlap area to determine $y(5)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Conclude that there is no overlap interval, so $x(\tau)h(5-\tau)=0$ everywhere and $y(5)=0$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Completes the overlap-area cases by showing that separated supports produce zero output rather than a positive or negative area.
solution_step_plan: Read the support interval of $x(\tau)$.
Read the support interval of $h(5-\tau)$.
State that the intervals do not overlap.
Conclude that the product is zero for every $\tau$.
State the convolution output value as zero.
practice_variation_axes: Vary which support interval lies to the left.
Vary the fixed output time label.
Vary the gap size.
Keep finite rectangular supports so no-overlap recognition is the central move.

sections.handoff_notes: Use this as the terminal contrast case: zero comes from no shared product interval, not from cancellation.
